title: Analyticity of Holomorphic Functions; Liouville and Morera

items.title: Locally uniform convergence on an open subset of the complex plane is compact convergence
Real-analytic maps between open subsets of the coordinate plane
The Taylor series of a holomorphic function at a point
The order of a zero of a holomorphic function
A holomorphic function equals its Taylor series throughout the largest centred disc in its domain
items.strategy: For a point a in an open set Omega, let rho be the distance from a to the complement, with rho=+infinity when Omega is the whole plane. Fix z with |z-a|<rho and choose a circle of radius r strictly between |z-a| and rho. Expand the Cauchy kernel on that circle by the finite geometric identity; its remainder tends uniformly to zero because |z-a|/r<1. Pass the uniform limit through the contour integral and use the higher-derivative Cauchy formula at a to identify the coefficient of (z-a)^n as f^(n)(a)/n!. Treat z=a and the whole-plane convention separately, and claim representation only on the largest disc contained in the given domain, not an exact convergence radius beyond it.

items.title: A complex function is holomorphic if and only if it is analytic
items.strategy: For the forward implication, apply the Taylor expansion theorem at every point to obtain a local convergent power-series representation. For the reverse implication, use the published theorem that every complex analytic function is holomorphic. State the equivalence on an arbitrary open set, including the empty set, and retain the same local domains in both directions.

items.title: Holomorphic functions are real analytic and smooth in their two real coordinates
items.strategy: Identify the complex plane with the coordinate plane. Expand the complex Taylor series at a and use the finite complex binomial theorem on h=x+iy. Absolute convergence for |x|+|y| below the complex radius licenses the total-degree real Taylor expansions of the real and imaginary parts, with the coefficients identified by repeated coordinate derivatives. For smoothness, use the real-linear derivative dictionary: repeated x- and y-partials are real and imaginary components of powers of i times the corresponding complex derivative; the higher complex derivatives exist and are holomorphic, hence continuous. Verify every mixed-derivative word, including the word of length zero.

items.title: Agreement of the power-series and Cauchy-integral formulas for Taylor coefficients
The order of a zero is the exponent in its local holomorphic factorization
items.strategy: If the order at a is finite m, the Taylor coefficients below m vanish and the m-th is nonzero. Factor (z-a)^m from the Taylor series and show directly that the shifted coefficient series converges on the same local disc; its sum g is analytic, hence holomorphic, and g(a) is the first nonzero Taylor coefficient, so continuity makes g nonzero nearby. Conversely expand a holomorphic g with g(a) nonzero and multiply by (z-a)^m to identify the first nonzero coefficient. Also prove that infinite order is equivalent to vanishing on a neighbourhood, without invoking the later identity theorem.

items.title: Cauchy's inequalities bound the Taylor coefficients by the circle supremum
items.strategy: On a circle of radius r compactly contained in the domain, write the n-th Taylor coefficient as f^(n)(a)/n!. Apply the published Cauchy inequality |f^(n)(a)|<=n! M/r^n and cancel n!. Include n=0, M=0, and require r>0 before division.

items.title: Liouville's theorem: every bounded entire function is constant
items.strategy: Let |f|<=M on the whole plane. At an arbitrary a, apply Cauchy's inequality with derivative order one on every positive radius r to obtain |f'(a)|<=M/r. If f'(a) were nonzero, choosing r>M/|f'(a)| would contradict the estimate. Thus f' vanishes everywhere, and the published zero-derivative theorem on the complex-plane domain makes f constant. Handle M=0 and the constant functions explicitly.

items.title: An entire function of polynomial growth is a polynomial
items.strategy: Assume |f(z)|<=C(1+|z|)^N with real C,N>=0. For every natural n>N, apply the Taylor-coefficient Cauchy estimate on the radius-R circle. For R>=1, bound (1+R)^N by 2^N R^N and let R grow; the exponential definition of real powers shows R^(N-n) tends to zero, forcing the n-th coefficient to vanish. The entire Taylor expansion therefore truncates after floor N. Treat C=0 and N=0, and use the integer-part inequalities to convert n>N into the exact degree bound.

items.title: The Liouville proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra
Morera's theorem: vanishing triangle integrals characterize holomorphy among continuous functions
items.strategy: For a continuous f on an open set with zero integral around every filled triangle contained in it, fix a point and a small disc with closure in the open set. The triangle-integral primitive construction on that star-shaped disc gives a holomorphic F with F'=f. The published higher-derivative theorem makes F' holomorphic, hence f is holomorphic near the chosen point. The converse is Goursat's triangle theorem. Keep continuity explicit, allow disconnected open sets, and prove both directions including degenerate triangles.

items.title: Cauchy estimates on a smaller concentric disc
items.strategy: Let 0<=r<R and suppose f is holomorphic on an open disc larger than the closed radius-R disc. Apply the higher-derivative Cauchy formula over the radius-R circle at each z with |z-a|<=r. The reverse triangle inequality gives |zeta-z|>=R-r; the ML estimate and circle length 2 pi R then yield |f^(n)(z)|<=n! R M/(R-r)^(n+1). Check n=0, r=0, M=0, and require r<R before every denominator.

items.title: Locally uniform limits of holomorphic functions are holomorphic and their derivatives converge locally uniformly
items.strategy: Use the compact-convergence dictionary to make the convergence uniform on every compact triangle and on a small closed disc around each point. The uniform limit theorem gives continuity, uniform passage through each triangle integral gives zero boundary integral, and Morera gives holomorphy of the limit. For derivative order k, choose nested concentric discs around a point and apply the subdisc Cauchy estimate to f_n-f; the outer-disc uniform error tends to zero, so the k-th derivative error tends uniformly to zero on the inner disc. This proves local uniform convergence for every natural k, including k=0.

items.title: A locally uniformly convergent series of holomorphic functions may be differentiated term by term
items.strategy: Apply the Weierstrass convergence theorem to the sequence of finite partial sums. Finite linearity of complex differentiation identifies the k-th derivative of each partial sum with the finite sum of the k-th derivatives. Passing to the locally uniform limit gives a holomorphic sum and the termwise derivative series for every natural k. Include the empty initial sum and k=0.

items.title: A jointly continuous finite-interval parameter integral of holomorphic functions is holomorphic
items.strategy: Let phi be jointly continuous on [a,b] times an open complex set and holomorphic in z for each parameter. Continuity gives the componentwise Riemann integral F(z). For a triangle compactly contained in the domain, parametrize its three edges and apply the real Riemann-Fubini theorem to the real and imaginary parts on each parameter-edge rectangle; interchange the parameter and contour integrals. Goursat makes every inner contour integral zero, so Morera makes F holomorphic. If the complex z-derivative of phi exists and is jointly continuous, use the complex fundamental theorem along a short z-segment and uniform continuity on a compact parameter-segment box to pass its difference quotient through the parameter integral, obtaining F'=integral of the derivative. Treat a=b separately and do not assert the derivative formula without the stronger joint-continuity hypothesis.

items.title: A holomorphic function equals its average on every compactly contained circle
items.strategy: Apply Cauchy's circle formula at the centre a of a positive-radius circle contained with its closed disc in the domain. Parametrize zeta=a+r exp(i theta), substitute d zeta=i r exp(i theta)d theta, and cancel the nonzero factors to obtain f(a)=(2 pi)^(-1) integral from 0 to 2 pi of f(a+r exp(i theta)). Check the positive orientation, r>0, and constant functions.

items.title: Every nonconstant entire function has dense image in the complex plane
items.strategy: If the image of an entire f is not dense, choose an open disc D(w,epsilon) disjoint from it. The reciprocal g=1/(f-w) is entire by the derivative algebra and satisfies |g|<=1/epsilon. Liouville makes g constant, hence f constant, a contradiction. Conversely no conclusion is claimed for constant functions. Make the positive missing-disc radius and the nonvanishing denominator explicit.

title: Analyticity of Holomorphic Functions; Liouville and Morera — Examples

items.title: $\sin z-z$ has a zero of order three at the origin
items.strategy: Use the published entire sine series to write sin z-z=-z^3/3!+z^5/5!-... near zero. The coefficient in degrees zero, one, and two vanishes and the degree-three coefficient is nonzero, so the order definition and factorization theorem give order three. Cross-check by differentiating three times at zero, including the signs and the value cos 0=1.

items.title: Morera proves holomorphy of $z\mapsto\int_0^1 t^z\,dt$ on $\operatorname{Re}z>1$
items.strategy: For t>0 use the principal power t^z=exp(z log t), and set 0^z=0 on the half-plane Re z>1. Each z-slice is entire for t>0 and identically zero for t=0. Near any parameter point, |t^z|=t^(Re z)<=t when 0<=t<=1, which proves joint continuity at t=0; continuity elsewhere follows from exponential and logarithm. Apply the parameter-integral theorem. The restriction Re z>1 is chosen so the endpoint extension is justified by the elementary bound t, rather than by an unstated improper-integral argument.

items.title: Uniform convergence on the closed unit disc does not give a holomorphic extension to a larger disc
items.strategy: Take F(z)=sum_{n>=1} z^n/n^2. The complex M-test and the p-series show uniform convergence on |z|<=1, while termwise differentiation on |z|<1 gives F'(r)=sum_{n>=1}r^(n-1)/n for real 0<r<1. For each large bound choose a harmonic partial sum above twice that bound, then choose r close enough to one that the corresponding finitely many powers exceed one half; hence F'(r) is unbounded as r approaches one. A holomorphic extension to any disc of radius greater than one would have continuous derivative bounded on the compact interval [0,1], a contradiction.

items.title: $z^n$ tends locally uniformly to zero on the unit disc but not uniformly on the closed disc
items.strategy: For a compact K in the open unit disc, continuity of modulus and compactness give q=max_{z in K}|z|<1. Then |z^n|<=q^n tends uniformly to zero on K. On the closed unit disc, the value at z=1 is one for every n, so uniform convergence to zero fails, indeed pointwise convergence to zero already fails there. Include K empty and n=0 without weakening the eventual estimate.

items.title: Morera's theorem fails without continuity
items.strategy: Let f be one at the origin and zero elsewhere. It is discontinuous at the origin and therefore not holomorphic. On every piecewise continuously differentiable triangle edge, changing the integrand at the finitely many parameter values mapping to the origin does not change its Riemann integral, so every triangle boundary integral is zero. This verifies every remaining Morera hypothesis and isolates continuity as essential; include triangles having an edge or vertex through the origin.

items.title: FALSE: every smooth map between open subsets of the plane is real analytic
items.strategy: Define phi(x)=exp(-1/x^2) for x nonzero and phi(0)=0, and F(x,y)=(phi(x),0). Repeated product and chain rules show every derivative of phi away from zero is a polynomial in 1/x times exp(-1/x^2); exponential domination makes every such derivative and the next difference quotient tend to zero at the origin. Thus F is smooth and every mixed derivative at (0,0) is zero. Its planar Taylor series there is the zero map, while F(x,0) is nonzero for x nonzero, so the defining local equality for real analyticity fails.

items.title: FALSE: an entire function bounded on the real axis is constant
items.strategy: Use complex sine. Its entire power series and derivative show it is nonconstant, while the real-restriction dictionary and the real trigonometric bound give |sin x|<=1 for every real x. This meets the weakened boundedness hypothesis and refutes the conclusion. Contrast only with Liouville's actual whole-plane boundedness hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: every entire function with an antiderivative is a polynomial
items.strategy: The complex exponential is entire and is its own antiderivative because exp'=exp. It never vanishes, since exp z exp(-z)=exp 0=1, and it is nonconstant because its derivative is nonzero. If it were a nonconstant polynomial, the published fundamental theorem of algebra would give a zero; if it were constant, its derivative would vanish. Thus it is an entire nonpolynomial with an antiderivative.
